title: The Best Way to Split Savings Between HYSA, CDs, and Treasury Bills
description: Optimizing your 'Cash Stack' for yield, liquidity, and taxes.
content:
Holding cash is no longer a passive activity. With interest rates hovering around 4-5%, your cash reserve can generate significant income. But where exactly should it go? A High-Yield Savings Account (HYSA) offers flexibility, CDs offer rate locks, and Treasury Bills offer tax advantages. Smart savers use all three. By splitting your cash into 'Liquidity', 'Income', and 'Tax-Efficient' buckets, you can squeeze an extra 0.5% - 1.0% yield out of your emergency fund without taking market risk.

Key Takeaways

  • HYSA for Speed: Keep 1-2 months of expenses here. The priority is instant access for bills, not maximum yield.
  • CDs for Certainty: Use CDs for money you need on a specific date (e.g., Wedding in 12 months). You lock in the rate so the Fed can't cut your income.
  • T-Bills for Efficiency: For amounts over $10,000, T-Bills are often superior to CDs because the interest is exempt from state/local taxes. This boosts your 'after-tax' return significantly.
  • The Ladder: Don't pick one duration. Build a ladder (3mo, 6mo, 1yr) to blend the benefits of all three.

Why It Matters (US Context)

If you live in a high-tax state (California, New York, Oregon), the tax-equivalent yield of a 5% T-Bill might beat a 5.5% CD. Always calculate the 'After-Tax Yield' before choosing.

The Allocation Framework

Scenario: You have $50,000 in cash savings.

Bucket 1: Immediate Access (20%)

Vehicle: High-Yield Savings (Ally/SoFi).
Amount: $10,000.
Role: Pay rent, credit card bills, unexpected car repairs.
Yield: ~4.2% (Variable).

Bucket 2: Rate Lock (40%)

Vehicle: 12-Month CD or CD Ladder.
Amount: $20,000.
Role: Locking in 4-5% yield even if the Fed cuts rates next month.
Yield: ~4.5% - 5.0% (Fixed).

Bucket 3: Tax Optimization (40%)

Vehicle: Short-Term Treasury Bills (4-week to 26-week).
Amount: $20,000.
Role: Maximizing after-tax return.
Yield: ~5.2% (State Tax Free).

When to Shift

  1. If Fed Raises Rates: Shift more to T-Bills/HYSA (Short Duration). You want to capture the rising rates quickly.
  2. If Fed Cuts Rates: Shift more to CDs (Long Duration). You want to lock in the old high rates before they disappear.
  3. If Moving States: If moving from Texas (No Tax) to California (High Tax), sell the CDs and buy T-Bills to shield income.
  4. Consolidation: Use a brokerage (Fidelity/Schwab) to hold the CDs and T-Bills in one place. It is easier than opening bank accounts at 5 different banks.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are T-Bills safe?

Yes. They are backed by the US Government. They are safer than bank accounts (which are backed by the FDIC, which is backed by the US Gov). T-Bills are the direct source of safety.

What is a 'No-Penalty' CD?

A hybrid. It locks the rate like a CD but allows withdrawal like a HYSA (after 7 days). Use this if you are unsure when you'll need the money.

Do I lose interest if I sell early?

With CDs, yes (penalty). With T-Bills, maybe (market price fluctuation). With HYSA, no. Liquidity has value.
